For V1 execution, Prelude focuses on the OpenAI + LiveKit path already integrated in the live interviewer runtime.

This benchmark remains useful, but it is no longer a blocker for the current V1 workflow. ElevenLabs should be treated as a challenger path for voice quality, latency and managed conversation features once the OpenAI path is stable enough to compare fairly.

## Goal

Benchmark OpenAI Realtime/voice path against ElevenLabs conversational/voice capabilities using the same Prelude interview scenarios and normalized event model.

The goal is not to choose the nicest demo voice. The goal is to decide whether ElevenLabs improves candidate comfort, latency, interruption handling or operational cost enough to justify provider complexity.

## Benchmark topology

```text
Candidate browser/mobile
  -> LiveKit room / WebRTC media
  -> Python LiveKit agent runtime
  -> Provider adapter: OpenAI OR ElevenLabs
  -> Go Realtime API
  -> Postgres live_interview_events + transcript reconstruction
```

- Normal direct answer.
- Long answer.
- Silence.
- Repeat request.
- Vague answer requiring one follow-up.
- Candidate interruption/barge-in.
- Noisy environment.
- Reconnect/provider failure.
- Closing after final answer.

## Metrics

- Time to first interviewer audio.
- Candidate speech end to interviewer response latency.
- Interruption/cancel latency.
- False interruption/backchannel rate.
- Transcript quality.
- Completed questions per run.
- Provider errors/reconnects.
- Cost per 5-minute interview.
- Subjective recruiter/candidate comfort score.
- Control over Prelude's state machine and compliance guardrails.

- Same interview plan and scripted candidate scenarios run against both providers.
- Runs persist normalized Prelude events and provider metadata separately.
- A report under docs/research summarizes metrics, subjective UX notes, costs, risks and recommendation.
- Recommendation states whether to stay OpenAI-only, add ElevenLabs as voice/challenger, or defer.

## Non-goals

- Blocking the current OpenAI V1 implementation.

value: |
  ## Challenge: Exact diagonalization benchmark for interacting Thouless pumps

  ### Summary

  This challenge uses exact diagonalization (ED) to study an interacting Thouless pump, using the spinful Rice--Mele--Hubbard chain as the minimal model. The goal is to compare four quantities:

  $$
  C_{\rm MB},\qquad
  \Delta_{\min},\qquad
  Q_{\rm adiabatic},\qquad
  Q_{\rm real\text{-}time}(T).
  $$

  Here \(C_{\rm MB}\) is the many-body Chern number, \(\Delta_{\min}\) is the minimum many-body gap during the pump cycle, \(Q_{\rm adiabatic}\) is the pumped charge inferred from polarization winding, and \(Q_{\rm real\text{-}time}(T)\) is the transported charge during a pump with finite period \(T\).

  The central question is:

  $$
  \textit{When do interactions preserve, destroy, or generate quantized Thouless pumping?}
  $$

  ### Physics motivation

  Thouless pumping is a classic example of quantized transport in one dimension. In the noninteracting Rice--Mele model, the pumped charge is determined by single-particle band topology. With Hubbard interactions, however, the problem becomes genuinely many-body: topology must be diagnosed using many-body eigenstates, gaps, Berry phases, and real-time dynamics.

  This topic is still active. Recent experiments and theory have studied Hubbard--Thouless pumps, interaction-induced breakdown of pumping, and interaction-enabled pumping in nonsliding lattices.

  Relevant references include:

  - D. J. Thouless, Phys. Rev. B 27, 6083 (1983).
  - A.-S. Walter et al., Nature Physics 19, 1471 (2023).
  - K. Viebahn et al., Phys. Rev. X 14, 021049 (2024).

  ### Model

  The baseline model is the spinful Rice--Mele--Hubbard chain,

  $$
  H(\phi)  =   -\sum_{j,\sigma}
  \left[t+(-1)^j\delta(\phi)\right]
  \left(c^\dagger_{j\sigma}c_{j+1,\sigma}+{\rm h.c.}\right)
  +
  \Delta(\phi)
  \sum_{j,\sigma}
  (-1)^j n_{j\sigma}
  +
  U\sum_j n_{j\uparrow}n_{j\downarrow}.
  $$

  A standard pump cycle is

  $$
  \delta(\phi)=\delta_0\cos\phi,
  \qquad
  \Delta(\phi)=\Delta_0\sin\phi,
  \qquad
  \phi:0\rightarrow 2\pi.
  $$

  The calculation should be performed in fixed particle-number sectors, for example at half filling,

  $$
  N_\uparrow=N_\downarrow=L/2.
  $$

  Suggested system sizes are \(L=6,8\) as mandatory targets, and \(L=10\) as an optional advanced target.

  ### Why exact diagonalization?

  ED is not the best method for large one-dimensional systems; DMRG/MPS is better for thermodynamic-limit ground states and long-time dynamics. However, ED is ideal here because it gives exact finite-size access to

  $$
  E_n(\theta,\phi),\qquad
  |\psi_n(\theta,\phi)\rangle,\qquad
  \langle \psi(\lambda)|\psi(\lambda+\Delta\lambda)\rangle,
  \qquad
  |\psi(t)\rangle.
  $$

  These are precisely the ingredients needed to compute many-body gaps, many-body Chern numbers, polarization winding, and exact finite-time pumped charge. ED should therefore be viewed as the exact small-system benchmark, while DMRG/MPS is the natural large-system follow-up.

  ### Key ED skills

  The implementation should pay careful attention to:

  - fermionic signs in the spinful occupation basis;
  - fixed \(N_\uparrow,N_\downarrow\) sectors;
  - twisted boundary conditions,
    \(c_{L+1,\sigma}=e^{i\theta}c_{1,\sigma}\);
  - gauge-invariant Berry curvature, for example using the Fukui--Hatsugai--Suzuki method;
  - minimum-gap tracking over the full \((\theta,\phi)\) parameter grid;
  - polarization phase unwrapping;
  - norm-conserving real-time evolution.

  ### Required measurements

  The solution should compute and compare:

  1. The low-energy spectrum \(E_n(\phi)\) and the minimum many-body gap
     \[
     \Delta_{\min}(U)=\min_{\theta,\phi}\left[E_1(\theta,\phi)-E_0(\theta,\phi)\right].
     \]

  2. The many-body Chern number \(C_{\rm MB}(U)\) on the \((\theta,\phi)\) torus.

  3. The many-body polarization \(P(\phi)\) and the adiabatic pumped charge \(Q_{\rm adiabatic}\).

  4. The finite-time pumped charge \(Q_{\rm real\text{-}time}(U,T)\).

  The key comparison is

  $$
  C_{\rm MB}
  \quad \text{versus} \quad
  Q_{\rm real\text{-}time}(T).
  $$

  This distinguishes true topological breakdown from finite-time nonadiabatic breakdown.

  ### Possible extensions

  Possible directions toward new physics include:

  - interaction-induced pumping, where the \(U=0\) system is trivial but finite \(U\) produces pumping;
  - adding nearest-neighbor repulsion \(V\) and mapping the \(U\)-\(V\) plane;
  - optimizing pump paths to maximize \(\Delta_{\min}\);
  - studying spin-charge diagnostics during the pump;
  - benchmarking the ED results against larger-system DMRG/MPS calculations.

  A possible paper-level goal is:

  $$
  \textit{Exact finite-size topology versus real-time transport in interacting Thouless pumps.}
  $$

### Released by

Zhongyi Ni, The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)

### Contact email

zni573@connect.hkust-gz.edu.cn

### Method

Quantum Circuit Simulation / Monte Carlo Simulation

### Challenge issue

## How much does atom reloading help loss-tolerant surface-code memory?

### Summary

Neutral-atom quantum computers are promising platforms for fault-tolerant quantum computation, but atom loss is a natural and potentially serious error source. If a physical qubit is lost during repeated syndrome extraction, the hardware site may remain vacant until the atom is reloaded or the logical information is moved away.

This challenge asks a concrete question:

**How much does active atom reloading improve the logical memory performance of a surface code under realistic loss and Pauli noise?**

The goal is to build a reproducible circuit-level Monte Carlo benchmark comparing different loss-handling and reloading policies.

### Physics motivation

Topological codes are known to be robust against detectable qubit loss, but neutral-atom devices introduce an additional operational question: after a qubit is lost, should the system reload it immediately, reload periodically, wait until too many atoms are missing, or avoid reloading during active error correction?

Reloading can reduce the accumulation of erased qubits, but it may also introduce timing overhead, reset errors, extra measurement rounds, or temporary code deformation. Quantifying this tradeoff is important for neutral-atom fault tolerance.

### Model

Use a rotated surface-code memory experiment with repeated stabilizer measurements.

Suggested mandatory targets:

- code distances \(d=3,5\);
- syndrome rounds \(T=d\) and \(T=2d\);
- data-qubit and measurement-qubit Pauli errors;
- stochastic atom-loss events;
- atom reloading with configurable interval or policy.

A minimal noise model should include:

1. Pauli data error probability \(p\);
2. measurement error probability \(p_m\);
3. atom-loss probability \(p_{\rm loss}\) per qubit per round;
4. reload interval \(R\), for example \(R=1,d,2d,\infty\);
5. optional reload failure or reset error probability.

### Challenge tasks

1. Simulate surface-code syndrome histories with atom loss.
2. Track missing qubits across rounds until they are reloaded.
3. Implement and compare several policies:
   - no reloading during the memory experiment;
   - periodic reloading every \(R\) rounds;
   - immediate reloading after detected loss;
   - threshold-triggered reloading when the missing-qubit fraction exceeds a chosen value.
4. Decode the resulting syndrome histories using a reasonable baseline decoder, for example MWPM with erasure information.
5. Measure:
   - logical error rate;
   - average number of missing qubits;
   - reload count / operational overhead;
   - sensitivity to \(p_{\rm loss}\), \(p\), \(p_m\), and \(R\).
6. Produce a regime map showing when reloading helps, when it is unnecessary, and when loss accumulation dominates.
7. Save the generated syndrome-history data in a decoder-ready format, so that future neural or learned decoders can be trained or evaluated on the same benchmark. This challenge does not require implementing or training an AI decoder.

### Decoder-ready data interface

Although this challenge does not require an AI decoder, the benchmark should define a simple data interface that future decoders can consume.

Each Monte Carlo shot should record at least:

- code distance \(d\);
- number of rounds \(T\);
- Pauli error parameters;
- loss probability and reload policy;
- detection-event or syndrome history;
- missing-qubit mask over space and time;
- reload events;
- final logical observable outcome.

A possible format is JSONL, HDF5, NPZ, or another documented array format. The key requirement is that a future decoder can treat the benchmark as:

```text
input: syndrome history + loss/reload history + metadata
output: predicted logical observable or correction class
```

This interface is only for benchmark portability. Training a neural decoder is out of scope for the summer-school challenge.

### Expected outcome

The expected output is a reproducible benchmark and a short report.

The report should include:

- logical-error-rate curves versus \(p_{\rm loss}\);
- comparison of no-reload, immediate-reload, and periodic-reload policies;
- plots of missing-qubit accumulation over time;
- discussion of the best reload interval \(R\) in different noise regimes;
- runtime and simulation-cost estimates;
- a documented decoder-ready data format for future learned decoders.

A useful headline result would be a plot showing how the pseudo-threshold or logical error rate changes as a function of the reload interval.

### Suggested verification

A valid implementation should include a small deterministic smoke test such as:

```bash
python -m reload_qec.verify \
  --fixture fixtures/d3_reload_accounting.json \
  --shots 1000 \
  --seed 13 \
  --out reports/reload_smoke.json
```

The verifier should print something like:

```text
PASS no_loss_reduction
PASS reload_accounting
PASS decoder_data_schema
PASS invalid_schedule_rejected
PASS report_written reports/reload_smoke.json
```

The checks should include:

1. **No-loss reduction:** when \(p_{\rm loss}=0\), changing the reload interval must not change the generated syndrome history or logical-failure count for a fixed random seed.
2. **Reload accounting:** for a deterministic fixture with one known atom loss, the no-reload policy must keep that site missing until the end, while the immediate-reload policy must restore it after the specified reload delay.
3. **Decoder-data schema:** the generated benchmark data must include syndrome history, missing-qubit mask, reload events, metadata, and logical outcome in a documented format.
4. **Negative control:** a fixture that requests reloading an invalid coordinate, or reloading before any atom has been lost, must be rejected rather than silently accepted.

### Possible extensions

- Train an AI decoder using the saved decoder-ready syndrome-history dataset.
- Compare learned decoders against erasure-aware MWPM on the same reload-policy benchmark.
- Add correlated atom-loss events.
- Add reload operations with finite success probability.
- Study code deformation or logical-qubit evacuation during array repair.
- Apply the benchmark to biased noise or neutral-atom native gate schedules.

### Out of scope

This challenge does not require training a neural network, implementing a graph neural network, or optimizing an AI decoder. The required deliverable is the loss/reloading simulation benchmark, baseline decoding, and a documented data interface that could support AI decoders in future work.

### Why this can lead to research output

This challenge isolates a practical fault-tolerance question for neutral-atom quantum computing: whether active hardware repair through atom reloading gives a real logical-level advantage, and what operational policy is best. The result would be useful both as a benchmark for future decoders and as guidance for neutral-atom architecture design.

### References

- T. M. Stace, S. D. Barrett, A. C. Doherty, *Thresholds for topological codes in the presence of loss*, arXiv:0904.3556, https://arxiv.org/abs/0904.3556.
- J. Vala, K. B. Whaley, D. S. Weiss, *Quantum Error Correction of a Qubit Loss in an Addressable Atomic System*, arXiv:quant-ph/0510021, https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/0510021.
- F. Kobayashi, S. Nagayama, *Erasure-tolerance scheme for the surface codes on neutral atom quantum computers*, arXiv:2404.12656, https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.12656.
- H. Perrin, G. Roger, G. Pupillo, *Correlated Atom Loss as a Resource for Quantum Error Correction*, arXiv:2603.24237, https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.24237.

### What happened?

`_issues_truncated: True` marks a frozen backlog as partial (the GitHub fetch hit its page cap).
`fetch_context_at` zeroes a truncated backlog at the source, but a frozen
`.vanguarstew_context.json` can still carry a partial `open_issues`/`open_prs` alongside the flag —
the "older frozen artifacts that still carry a partial backlog" case. Every consumer of the flag
fails closed on it as defense in depth so a partial backlog is not trusted:

- `agent/context.py::context_for_agent` zeroes `open_issues`/`open_prs` (its comment: *"Defense in
  depth for older frozen artifacts that still carry a partial backlog"*);
- `agent/planner.py::_safe_prs` drops the queue in reconciliation (#975);
- `benchmark/github_context.py::open_issues_from_context` returns `None` for backlog scoring.

`benchmark/baselines.py` — which builds the **reference opponent** the challenger is judged
against — reads the frozen `open_issues`/`open_prs` **directly** and is the only `_issues_truncated`
consumer without that guard. `run_replay` hands the same frozen `ctx` to both sides, so for such an
artifact the `queue_first`/`heuristic` baselines plan `"Review and merge PR: …"` / `"Address issue:
…"` items for a partial backlog the challenger's context has zeroed out. The pairwise judge then
compares them on inconsistent views, scoring the challenger worse for backlog/queue work it was
structurally denied — a skew driven purely by the truncation artifact.

### Steps to reproduce

```shell
python - <<'PY'
from benchmark import baselines as B
from agent.context import context_for_agent

# a frozen artifact carrying the flag with a partial backlog (the defense-in-depth case)
trunc = {"open_prs": [{"number": 5, "title": "Add OAuth login"}],
         "open_issues": [{"number": 9, "title": "Fix flaky test"}],
         "recent_commits": [{"subject": "fix: patch loader"}],
         "_issues_truncated": True}

qf = B.queue_first_plan(trunc, 5)
print("baseline reviews partial queue:", any(p["theme"] == "PR review queue" for p in qf))  # bug: True
print("challenger view open_prs:", context_for_agent(trunc)["open_prs"])                     # []
PY
```

### Area

benchmark (freeze / taskgen / judge / runner)

### Python version

3.11

### Relevant logs or output

```shell
baseline reviews partial queue: True
challenger view open_prs: []
```
title: baselines opponent does not honor _issues_truncated, so it exploits a partial backlog/queue the challenger's context zeroes out

## Summary

`benchmark/runner.py::run_replay` reads the agent's `solve()` output directly via `challenger.get("plan")` and `challenger.get("version_bump")` (in the objective-score and `trajectory_overlap` calls). The agent is miner-editable and untrusted, so `solve()` can return a **non-dict**. `_submission(challenger)` on the line above is already guarded for exactly this case (cf. #552 "guard _submission against non-dict agent output"), but these sibling `.get()` accesses are not — so a non-dict agent output raises `AttributeError` and aborts the entire replay batch instead of scoring that task as empty.

## Repro

An agent whose `solve()` returns a non-dict (a broken or adversarial miner agent):

```python
challenger = []          # e.g. solve(...) returned a list / string / None
challenger.get("plan")   # AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'get'
```

## Expected

Treat a non-dict agent output as empty — its fields degrade to `None`, which `objective_score(None, ...)` and `trajectory_overlap(None, ...)` already handle — and keep the run alive, consistent with the existing `_submission` guard. A single broken miner agent must not crash the benchmark.

## Where

`benchmark/runner.py::run_replay`

## Symptom

Every Community Benchmark upload from the Throughput Benchmark tab fails. The upload panel renders the full Cloudflare "Just a moment..." challenge HTML interstitial as the error message for each `pp{N}` row. `0/N uploaded` is the consistent result. Behavior is reproducible:

- Across two different Macs (MacBook + Mac Studio) on different networks
- Against the stock oMLX DMG release (no fork modifications)
- For at least the past several weeks (regression of unknown date)

## Reproduction (network-level, no oMLX needed)

```bash
$ curl -i -X POST https://omlx.ai/api/benchmarks \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{}'

HTTP/2 403
cf-mitigated: challenge
content-type: text/html; charset=UTF-8
content-length: 5290
server: cloudflare
server-timing: chlray;desc="9fa3b5aac93e012e"
...

<!DOCTYPE html><html lang="en-US"><head><title>Just a moment...</title>...
```

Headers and body confirm a **Cloudflare Managed Challenge** (`cf-mitigated: challenge`). The challenge fires for every `POST` to `/api/benchmarks` regardless of `User-Agent`:

| UA | Status |
|---|---|
| `python-requests/2.32.5` (oMLX's actual UA) | 403 |
| Safari macOS UA | 403 |
| Chrome macOS UA | 403 |

`GET /api/benchmarks` also returns 403, so the endpoint is fully gated rather than just POST-restricted.

## Diagnosis

The omlx.ai infrastructure has Cloudflare protection (Bot Fight Mode or Managed Challenge) enabled on `/api/benchmarks`. Because oMLX's upload client (`requests.post` in `omlx/admin/benchmark.py:_upload_to_omlx_ai`) cannot solve a JS challenge, every submission gets rejected before it reaches the API.

This is **not** an oMLX client bug. The client is well-formed — it sends a single JSON `POST` with reasonable headers. Cloudflare is just blocking the entire class of non-browser API traffic.

That said, oMLX **did** have a related client-side bug: the error path piped the entire HTML challenge body into the dashboard's SSE error event, where `<span x-text="r.error">` rendered the markup as the error message. Filed as PR #1192 (sanitize the error string so the panel surfaces a one-line actionable message instead of a 5KB markup blob).

## Suggested resolution paths (server-side — you'd know best)

In rough order of effort:

1. **Allow-list `/api/benchmarks` in the omlx.ai Cloudflare config** — add a WAF skip rule for `POST /api/benchmarks` with appropriate rate limiting. Lowest-friction option.
2. **Move the benchmark API to a separate origin/subdomain** that isn't behind the challenge layer (e.g. `api.omlx.ai/benchmarks` without managed challenge).
3. **Switch to API-key auth** — issue keys to oMLX clients (e.g. tied to the `owner_hash`) and configure Cloudflare to bypass challenge when a valid API key header is present.
4. **Add a token-exchange endpoint** that returns a short-lived signed token after the client passes Cloudflare's Turnstile/JS challenge, then submit the actual benchmark with that token. More complex but preserves bot protection.

Happy to test against any of the above from this environment if useful.

## Impact

Community benchmark contributions have been silently failing for an extended period — leaderboard volume on omlx.ai is presumably depressed because of this. Users see a broken upload panel on every run, which (without PR #1192) is also unreadable.

## Related

- PR #1192 (client-side UI fix only — sanitizes the error display so users get a one-line message instead of the raw CF interstitial)
- PR #1052 (open, by @jabagawee — makes upload opt-in; would let users hide the symptom but doesn't fix the underlying upload failure)
title: Community benchmark uploads fail with HTTP 403 — omlx.ai/api/benchmarks gated by Cloudflare challenge

Clone `scifact_chunk_eval.py` → `bioasq_eval.py`, reusing:

- The **7 chunking configs**, isolated `bioasq_m7_*` Qdrant+ES stores (prefix guard on teardown), tenant `public`.
- `HybridRetriever` (dense + BM25 RRF) + crossencoder rerank; chunks collapsed to `doc_id` (best-rank-first).
- **Doc-level BEIR metrics** (nDCG@10 primary, recall@{10,100}, MAP) + the paired-bootstrap CIs / Wilcoxon-Holm significance layer.
- **3-tier loader**: HF `datasets` (gated) → `beir` lib (manual `data_folder`) → `ir_datasets` (`beir/bioasq`).

### Scale caveat (must handle)

BEIR's BioASQ corpus is **~15M passages** (~500 test queries) — a very different ingest from SciFact's 5,183. ### Bonus (follow-on)

BioASQ ships **snippet-level judgments + reference answers** → enables both passage-level retrieval eval *and* end-to-end answer-quality (RAGAS-style faithfulness/attribution) on the same data — closest mirror to the production workload.

If BioASQ access stalls, **NFCorpus** and **TREC-COVID** are ✅ public biomedical BEIR datasets usable as an immediate #2 with zero access friction.

The "intent gap" — the distance between an informal natural language requirement and a checkable formal specification — is identified as the central challenge for reliable AI-generated code (arXiv:2603.17150), yet no standard benchmark measures how well a system formalizes intent. A critical bottleneck is validating specification quality: current proxies (test pass rate, BLEU against reference specs) do not capture whether specifications actually reflect user intent.

We need a benchmark that presents the same vague requirement to multiple specification strategies (lightweight tests, formal assertions, DSL synthesis) and measures: (1) semantic coverage via execution traces against edge cases, (2) false-positive rate from over-constrained specs, and (3) alignment with held-out user acceptance criteria collected through user studies.

**Key references:** arXiv:2603.17150 (Intent Formalization Grand Challenge)

**Success metric:** Semantic coverage rate on held-out edge cases; false-positive rate from over-specification; alignment score vs. user acceptance criteria.
title: Closing the intent gap: benchmarks for intent formalization quality

As an operator reviewing benchmark work, I want to record each engineering attempt against an AOC assignment so I can see who worked on what, which pull request they opened, and what review state the attempt is currently in.

7. The form clears after a successful submit.
8. If the form is invalid, I stay on the dashboard.
9. My entered values remain visible.
10. Each invalid field shows its own error message.
11. The existing run list remains visible.
12. If I refresh the page, previously created runs are still visible.

### Abstract

Recently, Large Language models (LLMs) find application in several fields. This extends to hardware definition and synthesis. However, most works at the intersection of LLMs and hardware generation focus on text-based tasks, creating a gap for multi-modal LLMs for RTL design. In this work, we introduce MultModLM, a benchmark for evaluating LLMs on the task of generating hardware schematics from RTL (Register Transfer Level) descriptions. The dataset consists of 99 diverse RTL modules spanning arithmetic, control, and state-based designs. To address the challenges of non-unique schematic representations, we propose a multi-stage evaluation framework combining rubric-based scoring, self-evaluation, cross-model assessment, blind evaluation, and human validation to enable exhaustive evaluation.
  Through experiments on state-of-the-art LLMs, we observe that while models can generate visually interpretable schematics, their functional correctness remains constrained. Furthermore, we find that LLM-based evaluators exhibit near-zero agreement with human raters, revealing, as a key finding, that LLM-as-a-judge paradigms are unreliable in structurally precise domains. These findings suggest that reliable evaluation of multi-modal hardware outputs remains an open challenge, motivating the need for more robust and domain-aware evaluation methodologies, as well as tools for structural evaluation, so as to enable formal equivalence checkers.

Hi -- one clarification on the challenge -- the ICCAD04 test cases are clustered (standard cells grouped together).  This is not the "classic" version of the problem, from Markov's ICCAD04 paper.
https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/stamp/stamp.jsp?tp=&arnumber=1382639

In the original work, there are both macro blocks and (lots of) standard cells.  The early placement tools produced legal placements for everything, all the way down to the standard cells.  The ICCAD04 benchmark set was a variation of an earlier ISPD02 set (in ICCAD04, the macro blocks went from square to rectangular, and there was some adjustment of pin locations).  The ISPD02 set is based on Chuck Alpert's ISPD98 partitioning benchmarks. 

The clustered formulation is how most modern tools do things; macro placement first, followed by standard cell placement in the gaps and open spaces.  The challenge formulation is the right way to go, but different than how things were done in the early days!  I'm mentioning the difference, as it seems to get overlooked.  I've run across stacks of recent papers which seem to compare clustered (and non-legalized) wire length numbers to non-clustered and fully legal placements -- an apples-to-oranges comparison, leading to incorrect conclusions.
title: ICCAD04 benchmark variation

## Summary

`verify_submission_result()` (`kata/submissions.py`) treats a challenge result as belonging to the submission under verification when only these match:

1. `summary.mode == validation.metadata.mode`
2. `summary.candidate_artifact_hash == hash_submission_bundle(submission_path)`

It does **not** check that `summary.candidate_artifact` resolves to the same path as `submission_path`, nor that lane `challenge_state.candidate_submission_id` matches `validation.metadata.submission_id`.

Because artifact hashing is content-only, two different submission directories with identical `agent.py` produce the same hash. A PR can point `verify`/`decide`/`promote` at submission B while supplying `challenge_summary.json` from submission A's winning run. If king/benchmark are still current, `auto_merge_ready` becomes true and the wrong submission can be promoted.

This breaks the documented auto-merge invariant: *"Before a merge, the result is re-checked against the current submission payload."* Hash equality is necessary but not sufficient.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Run a winning duel for submission A under `submissions/<pack>/<mode>/alice-.../`.
2. Copy the same `agent.py` into a second submission B with a different `submission_id` (same content hash).
3. Call `verify_submission_result(str(submission_B), summary_path_from_A)`.

## Expected behavior

Verification fails: `submission_matches_challenge` is false and `auto_merge_ready` is false because the challenge summary was produced for a different submission identity.

## Actual behavior

Verification succeeds when hashes match, even though `summary.candidate_artifact` and lane `candidate_submission_id` refer to submission A.

## Context

`ChallengeSummary` already records `candidate_artifact` (path), and lane `ChallengeState` records `candidate_submission_id` — both are unused during verification. `tests/test_submissions.py` covers stale benchmark/king cases but not cross-submission hash collision. Per `CONTRIBUTING.md`, this is an evaluator correctness / promotion safety issue.

PR to follow.

The track parameter validation hook (introduced in #2144) runs validators as part of `rally race`, inside the actor system, just before the benchmark starts. This means a bad parameter is only reported after Rally bootstraps the actor system, and the error is shown as a traceback rather than a clean message.

The proposal is to run the validators in the main process before the actor system starts, reusing the existing `params.invoke_validators` seam. Load the track, resolve the challenge, and run the validators. On success, print a short confirmation (e.g. "Track parameters for challenge [<name>] are valid.") and exit zero; on failure, exit non-zero with the TrackConfigError message. This keeps the check fast, avoids any cluster contact, and gives a clean one-line error.

## Problem / motivation

The benchmark exists to decide *whether an agent is good enough to prefer over the reference*, and the M2 acceptance is explicit: **"an agent that merely restates a memorized outcome does not win."** Today `run_eval` reports the raw numbers - `composite_mean`, `decisive_margin`, judge stats - but the actual **decision** ("is this run good enough to promote the challenger?") is made by eye. There is no reproducible, CI-gateable rule.

## Proposed solution

Add a **pass/fail promotion gate** over a `run_replay` / `run_multi_replay` result:

- `check_promotion(result, .)` evaluates four named criteria: the run completed with a scored composite; `composite_mean` clears `min_composite`; the challenger **decisively** beat the baseline (`decisive_margin >= min_decisive_margin`, so a memorized-tie agent that doesn't out-decide the reference fails); and the pairwise judge is trustworthy (order-`disagreement_rate <= max_disagreement`, with a single-order run passing for lack of an instability signal).
- `decisive_margin` is taken from the field or derived from the aggregate `tally`, so it works for single- and multi-repo results.
- `scripts/promotion.py --strict` exits non-zero on HOLD - gating promotion in CI the way `--fail-under` gates a score.

Robust: pure evaluation, never mutate the result, malformed/non-dict results fail the relevant checks rather than raising.

## Acceptance criteria

- A strong run promotes; a below-floor composite, a non-decisive margin (tie), high judge disagreement, or an errored run each fails its check (others still reported).
- `decisive_margin` derived from `tally` when the field is absent; thresholds configurable.
- Malformed/non-dict/non-numeric results fail gracefully.
- `scripts/promotion.py --strict` exits non-zero on HOLD.
- Offline tests cover each criterion and edge cases.

## Area

benchmark (evaluation / CI promotion gating)
title: Gate whether a run promotes the challenger agent (decisive-win + quality gate, CI exit code)

Objective

This issue invites adversarial review of Proposition 7 and the Contestability Layer introduced in A-DAP.

The goal is not to defend the proposition.

The goal is to falsify it.

---

Proposition 7

There exist systems S such that:

NDC(S) > 1

while

CEI-Effective(S, A, I) = 0

where:

- S = system
- A = affected party
- I = institutional context

Therefore:

Independent verifiability is necessary but not sufficient for effective contestability.

---

What We Are Looking For

Counterexamples.

Specifically:

Case A

A system where:

- NDC(S) > 1
- CEI-Effective(S, A, I) > 0

but Proposition 7 predicts otherwise.

Case B

A system where:

- CEI-Effective(S, A, I) > 0
- NDC(S ∪ I) = 1

without hidden independent verification paths.

Case C

Evidence that one of the proposed contestability layers collapses into another and should not be treated as a separate analytical category.

**Authors:** Dhruv Kulkarni, Sai Manoj Pudukotai Dinkarrao
**Published:** 2026-06-26
**Categories:** `cs.AR`

**Links:** [abs](http://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27666v1) | [pdf](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.27666v1)

---

### Abstract

Recently, Large Language models (LLMs) find application in several fields. This extends to hardware definition and synthesis. However, most works at the intersection of LLMs and hardware generation focus on text-based tasks, creating a gap for multi-modal LLMs for RTL design. In this work, we introduce MultModLM, a benchmark for evaluating LLMs on the task of generating hardware schematics from RTL (Register Transfer Level) descriptions. The dataset consists of 99 diverse RTL modules spanning arithmetic, control, and state-based designs. To address the challenges of non-unique schematic representations, we propose a multi-stage evaluation framework combining rubric-based scoring, self-evaluation, cross-model assessment, blind evaluation, and human validation to enable exhaustive evaluation.
  Through experiments on state-of-the-art LLMs, we observe that while models can generate visually interpretable schematics, their functional correctness remains constrained. Furthermore, we find that LLM-based evaluators exhibit near-zero agreement with human raters, revealing, as a key finding, that LLM-as-a-judge paradigms are unreliable in structurally precise domains. These findings suggest that reliable evaluation of multi-modal hardware outputs remains an open challenge, motivating the need for more robust and domain-aware evaluation methodologies, as well as tools for structural evaluation, so as to enable formal equivalence checkers.

## RoboWits: Unexpected Challenges for Robotic Creative Problem Solving

**Authors:** Chunru Lin, Hongxin Zhang, Fenghao Yu, Zhehuan Chen, Thomas L. Griffiths, Yejin Choi, David Held, Chuang Gan
**Published:** 2026-05-28
**Categories:** `cs.RO`, `cs.AI`

**Links:** [abs](http://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30326v1) | [pdf](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.30326v1)

---

### Abstract

The ability to reason, adapt, and creatively solve problems under unexpected challenges is essential for robots operating in real-world environments. However, current robotic benchmarks primarily emphasize skill-level execution and provide limited insight into such cognitive reasoning capabilities. We introduce RoboWits, a bi-manual robotic benchmark designed to systematically evaluate cognitive reasoning, creative tool use, and robustness to unexpected conditions. To enable scalable construction of high-quality reasoning-centric unexpected scenarios, we propose an automated task generation pipeline formulated as a multi-agent cooperative framework, comprising agents for seed task generation and verification, metric generation, scene generation, and task mutation. Using the pipeline, we curated 30 diverse seed tasks and 208 tasks with mutations and graded difficulty across geometry, material, and assembly-based reasoning. We benchmark popular robot policies, pre-trained VLAs, and oracle-state planners. Our results reveal a significant performance gap: while pre-trained VLAs exhibit preliminary success on seed tasks after single-task fine-tuning, they struggle to perform on mutated tasks, implying their brittleness in manipulation tasks requiring reasoning, strategy adaptation, and robustness to deceptive or constrained environments. Project page is available at https://umass-embodied-agi.github.io/RoboWits.
title: [2605.30326v1] RoboWits: Unexpected Challenges for Robotic Creative Problem Solving

## Summary

Add **science and commonsense QA** benchmarks in Basque. This covers a cluster of tasks that probe a model's ability to apply physical, social, and scientific knowledge — complementing the factual recall of EusTrivia and the language-form focus of BasqueGLUE.

## Dataset Candidates

Four candidates from the TODO backlog, all part of the same Basque adaptation effort:

| ID | Candidate path | Task | Format |
|----|---------------|------|--------|
| `ARC_eu_easy` | `arc_eu_easy_mc` | Elementary science QA (easy) | 4-way MC |
| `ARC_eu_challenge` | `arc_eu_challenge_mc` | Elementary science QA (hard) | 4-way MC |
| `PIQA_eu` | `piqa_eu_mc` | Physical intuition QA | 2-way MC |
| `SIQA_eu` | `siqa_eu_mc` | Social interaction QA | 3-way MC |

**Recommended rollout order**: ARC Easy → ARC Challenge → PIQA → SIQA. ARC is the most established and directly comparable to international benchmarks.

## Motivation

### ARC (AI2 Reasoning Challenge)
ARC tests grade-school science knowledge. The **Easy** split covers straightforward factual science questions; the **Challenge** split is specifically designed to defeat retrieval-based and word co-occurrence models — requiring genuine reasoning. Both together form a complete difficulty gradient and are among the most widely cited benchmarks in the multilingual NLP literature, enabling direct external comparisons.

### PIQA (Physical Intuition QA)
PIQA tests whether a model understands how physical objects behave and how to accomplish everyday physical tasks (e.g., "How do you remove a stripped screw?"). This capability — physical commonsense — is well-documented as a weakness for LLMs in low-resource settings. The internal docs reference **BasPhyCo** as evidence that Basque LLMs specifically struggle here.

### SIQA (Social Interaction QA)
SIQA tests social commonsense: understanding motivations, reactions, and consequences of human social behaviour. This is orthogonal to all current benchmarks and tests a model's cultural and pragmatic reasoning in Basque.

This issue tracks **all four benchmarks as a group** since they likely share the same dataset repository and schema. They should be implemented together to avoid repeated dataset inspection overhead.

All four are expected to be **JSON-only specs** (no plugins) if:
- Field names are standard (`question`, `choices`/`candidates`, `answer` as int index)

- SIQA (3-way): same template, adapted to A/B/C

## The scenario

|---|---|---|

## 🛠️ AI Developer track

Welcome. This is not a trick test. It is a small, real piece of the work we do every day in the Venture Studio and n8n CoE: building something useful quickly with AI.

There is no model solution you need to match. We look at how you break down an underspecified problem, make decisions, and use AI meaningfully.

### Mission

Build an **ESG-Radar**: a small pipeline that reads in sustainability disclosures, scores the KPIs against sector benchmarks, identifies gaps and risks, and outputs a concise readiness report with prioritised actions.

We provide a seed dataset with sample companies (`disclosures.json` / `disclosures.csv`), sector benchmarks (`benchmarks.json`), and a few individual profiles. No domain knowledge needed — all fields are documented ([`../data/README.md`](../data/README.md)) and everything you need is in the dataset.

> 📂 **In the repo:** [`../data/`](../data/) with `disclosures.json`, `disclosures.csv`, `benchmarks.json`, and sample profiles (field docs: [`../data/README.md`](../data/README.md)). Seed dataset, synthetic/simplified, as of 2026-06, not an official AI:AT position.

### Part A: Build the PoC

- **Input:** one or more disclosures (one company per record: industry, sector, GHG emissions Scope 1/2/3, energy and renewable share, female leadership ratio, headcount, accident rate) plus the matching sector benchmarks.
- **Output:** a reasoned readiness report per company: a score (scale is your decision — justify it briefly), a "above/below benchmark, because…" statement per KPI, and 2–3 prioritised actions for the biggest gaps.
- **Form:** a runnable Git repo with real Python code, plus a README that gets us up and running in under 5 minutes.

> **The interesting design decision:** The KPIs are not directly comparable. Emissions are given as absolute tonnes (`ghg_scope1_t_co2e` etc.), while the benchmark is expressed as intensity per employee (`benchmark_ghg_intensitaet_t_co2e_pro_ma`). How you normalise, which KPIs you start with, how you handle missing values (e.g. `ghg_scope3 = null`, unknown sector), and how you weight the KPIs into a score — that is exactly where we see your judgment. We care about the reasoning, not a prescribed formula.

> A real LLM call (e.g. for the action recommendation texts) is allowed but not required. A deterministic or template-based report is perfectly fine, and no API key is needed if you don't have one. Stack: Python ≥ 3.11 (libraries freely chosen).

### Part B: Code review (~15 min)

We give you a short, AI-generated Python snippet ([`code-review/snippet.py`](./dev/code-review/snippet.py)). Tip: compare what the doc-comment *promises* with what the code *does*, and pay attention to units. There is one central functional bug. Find it, fix it, and justify in 3–5 sentences why it is a bug. Also tell us what else you notice — missing edge cases, questionable assumptions, missing validation. That wider critique counts just as much as the fix itself. We want to see whether you can *evaluate* AI output, not just generate it.

> The snippet is in the file [`./dev/code-review/snippet.py`](./dev/code-review/snippet.py). Do not reproduce the code in your submission — a clear written explanation is sufficient.

You research or estimate the number of reachable customers, the price, and conversion yourself — AI and the web are there exactly for that (sources welcome). For this analysis, treat ESG-Radar as a standalone commercial venture, separate from the (non-commercial, EU-funded) AI:AT context.

### What happened?

`check_sample_adequacy` gates whether a run "judged and accounted for enough tasks" — its
`all_tasks_decided` check verifies the challenger/baseline/tie tally sums to the task total, so no
task vanished between judging and tallying. Its `_total_tasks` helper is multi-repo aware (it sums
each `per_repo` entry's `tasks` across `_partition_entries`), but its sibling `_decided` reads the
tally from **one place only** — `result.get("tally")` (top-level).

`run_multi_replay` / `run_generalization_report` artifacts have **no top-level `tally`**: the
per-task tally lives under each `per_repo[i]["tally"]` (the aggregate is under `judge_report`). So
for **every** real multi-repo / generalization run, `_decided` returns `None`, `all_tasks_decided`
fails closed, and the run is verdicted **INADEQUATE** — even when every task was decided. Since the
module's job is to stop an inadequate sample from flowing into `compare_eval` / `trend` / a
leaderboard "as if it were as solid as a full run," this permanently flags every cross-repo and M3
generalization run.

The existing tests miss it because they only reach `all_tasks_decided` passing by injecting a
**synthetic top-level `tally`** (`dict(_multi(...), tally={...})`) — a shape real runs never emit.

### Steps to reproduce

```shell
python - <<'PY'
from benchmark.sample_adequacy import check_sample_adequacy, _total_tasks, _decided
# real run_multi_replay shape: no top-level tally; per_repo carries the tallies
multi = {"per_repo": [
    {"repo": "a", "tasks": 5, "tally": {"challenger": 4, "baseline": 1, "tie": 0}},
    {"repo": "b", "tasks": 5, "tally": {"challenger": 3, "baseline": 1, "tie": 1}},
]}
print("total_tasks:", _total_tasks(multi))   # 10 (correct)
print("decided:", _decided(multi))           # bug: None
print("passed:", check_sample_adequacy(multi)["passed"])  # bug: False (INADEQUATE)
PY
```

### Area

benchmark (freeze / taskgen / judge / runner)

### Python version

3.11

### Relevant logs or output

```shell
total_tasks: 10
decided: None
passed: False
```
title: check_sample_adequacy verdicts every multi-repo/generalization run INADEQUATE: _decided reads only a top-level tally that cross-repo runs never emit

## Problem

Replay artifacts report judge outcomes through `tally`, `decisive_margin`, and per-task `rows`. Promotion, regression, and leaderboard tooling consume those fields, but nothing verifies they agree. A hand-edited artifact could inflate `decisive_margin` while per-task rows tell a different story.

## Proposal

Add `benchmark/tally_integrity.py` and `scripts/tally_integrity.py` that verify, for each scored replay slice:

- `tally` carries numeric challenger/baseline/tie counts that sum to `tasks`

## Summary

Ingest the [Kaggle Morse Learning Machine Challenge v2](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/morse-learning-machine-challenge-v2) dataset as a **third external benchmark** alongside `training-set-a` (real OTA) and the adversarial synthetic suite (PR #417). Use it to (a) get a defensible external metric for our decoder, (b) cross-validate the `augment-arrl` (PR TBD) augmentation distributions, and (c) stress-test wider WPM range than our current suites cover.

## Dataset facts

- 200 WAV files, mono, 32-bit float, 8 kHz
- ~100 labeled (training, in `SampleSubmission.csv`); ~100 unlabeled (validation, scored via submission)
- Per-file randomization:
  - SNR: -14 to +20 dB
  - Pitch: 600 - 1200 Hz
  - Speed: 12 - 80 WPM
- Filename convention: `cw001.wav` ... `cw200.wav`
- Scoring metric: Levenshtein distance (== our CER, conveniently)

Reference baseline solution: https://github.com/talengu/kaggle_morse

## Why it matters

1. **External metric.** We have been grading our own homework on a 6-sample real OTA bench (training-set-a). The Kaggle leaderboard gives us a public, third-party number — useful for sanity checking and as a defensible "v1 done" signal.
2. **Augmentation distribution validation.** The competition's `(SNR ∈ [-14,+20], WPM ∈ [12,80], pitch ∈ [600,1200])` is exactly what `augment-arrl` is synthesizing. If our augmented corpus does not bracket the Kaggle distribution, our augmenter is mis-tuned. Cheap to check via histogram overlay.
3. **WPM stress test.** Our current bench tops out at 40 WPM. The Kaggle 50-80 WPM tail is something we never exercise. The two-pass WPM seed (PR #423) needs to be re-validated at high WPM since the bias-correction constants were tuned at 13-40 WPM.
4. **Independent overfitting check.** If we only optimize for training-set-a + adversarial-suite, we will silently overfit those distributions. Kaggle is held-out by construction.

## What this is NOT

- Not a training corpus. ~100 labeled files is too small for neural training. Our augmented ARRL corpus (~535 h, ~47k variants from `augment-arrl`) dwarfs it by 3+ orders of magnitude.
- Not "real world" — synthetic CW + AWGN, no Watterson channel, no QRM, no human fist variability. Beating Kaggle is necessary but not sufficient for OTA performance.
- Competition is closed (no prize), but the leaderboard still accepts submissions for scoring.

## Acceptance criteria

1. **Ingest pipeline**:
   - Script to download dataset (Kaggle CLI auth required) under `data/cw-samples/kaggle-morse-v2/` (gitignored).
   - Manifest at `experiments/cw-decoder/scripts/kaggle_morse_v2/manifest.jsonl` mapping file -> truth (where labeled).
   - Reuse the existing `bench.py` harness; emit per-file CER + aggregate stats.

2. **Baseline run**: Score current best (viterbi from PR #411 + wpm-seed-fix from PR #423) on the 100 labeled training samples. Report mean / median / p95 CER, broken down by SNR bucket and WPM bucket.

3. **Submission**: Generate a submission CSV from the 100 unlabeled validation samples and submit to the leaderboard. Capture the leaderboard score in the report.

4. **Distribution cross-validation** (depends on `augment-arrl` landing): overlay our augmented corpus distributions against Kaggle's per-file (SNR, WPM, pitch) statistics. Flag any mismatch.

5. **Regression check**: confirm the PR #423 wpm-seed-fix gate behaves correctly at high WPM (50-80). Specifically check:
   - Is the histogram bias correction (`frame_len + frame_step` ≈ 35 ms) still appropriate at 80 WPM dit length (~15 ms)?
   - Does the dit/dah concentration gate fire correctly when both clusters are sub-30 ms?

6. **Honest report** with:
   - Per-SNR-bucket CER table
   - Per-WPM-bucket CER table
   - Failure-mode analysis on the worst 10 files (paste decoded vs truth)
   - Comparison: our score vs published `talengu/kaggle_morse` baseline (CNN+LSTM, ~2018-era)
   - Recommendation: any concrete decoder changes needed to reduce the high-WPM or low-SNR error rate

## Sequencing

This depends on:
- PR #411 (viterbi) and PR #423 (wpm-seed-fix) merged so we have a stable best-of-bake-off baseline to evaluate
- `augment-arrl` (PR TBD) for the distribution cross-validation step

Can begin ingest + baseline run as soon as #411 and #423 land. Distribution check waits on `augment-arrl`.

## Risks

- **Kaggle ToS**: dataset license must be checked before redistributing or training models from it. Likely "competition use only" — that's fine for in-repo benchmarking, but flag for the LLM-repair experiment (#422) which would consume training pairs.
- **Kaggle CLI auth**: requires per-developer Kaggle API token. Document setup in the script.
- **Dataset is synthetic**: do not over-weight Kaggle results — they validate decoder robustness across SNR/WPM but tell us nothing about Watterson channel, QRM, or fist variation.

## Open design questions

1. Submit to the leaderboard? It's public and our score becomes visible. Probably yes — gives us a citation-grade external number.
2. Use the 100 labeled files as additional regression bench, or hold them out for distribution validation only?
3. The published `talengu/kaggle_morse` baseline uses CNN+LSTM. Worth mining for ideas / weights / architecture before our `augment-arrl` + neural work?

CodeHalu introduces "execution-based verification" as the ground truth for code hallucination: rather than judging generated code by surface similarity to a reference solution, the CodeHaluEval benchmark (8,883 samples across 699 tasks) actually *runs* the generated code and classifies failures into a hallucination taxonomy (e.g., mapping, naming, resource, logic hallucinations) based on divergent execution behavior. This is the code-domain instance of the same design pattern finance is converging on — separating a fluent LLM (candidate generation / narrative) from a deterministic executor (symbolic/runtime verification) — directly paralleling AUDITFLOW's re-execution of accounting calculations and FinChain's executable-Python CoT verification in \S\ref{sec:llm-analysis}. Separately, industry surveys cited alongside this benchmark note that roughly 20% of AI-suggested package names in generated code do not exist (a "dependency hallucination" supply-chain risk), and that mitigation techniques can reduce measured hallucination rates by up to 96% when execution verification is added to the generation loop.

**Source:** arXiv:2405.00253, "CodeHalu: Investigating Code Hallucinations in LLMs via Execution-based Verification" (2024)
**Link:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.00253

## Summary

The gstack-codex `challenge` mode surfaced **9 substantive findings** on PR #147 that relay-review's 6 sequential rounds missed — including real production bypasses (file deletion after dispatch, path escape, branch-reuse manifest inheritance, skip-path rubric bypass) and a sharp critique of compliance-theater rounds.

Relay-review is currently collaborative-critical (find issues the executor should fix). gstack-codex challenge is adversarial (try to break it; think like an attacker; no compliments). Different mode, different yield. Benchmark the style difference and decide which pieces to adopt.

## Observed style difference (empirical, from PR #147)

| Dimension | relay-review (6 rounds) | gstack-codex challenge (1 pass) |
|-----------|-------------------------|---------------------------------|
| Findings that were genuine code gaps | 4 rounds × 1-3 issues | 9 findings in 1 pass |
| Bypass vectors found | 0 explicit | 4 (file delete, path escape, branch reuse, skip-path) |
| Test-suite critique | 0 | "suite mostly proves bypasses work, not enforcement" |
| Compliance-theater detection | 0 (round 5 was theater, reviewer acknowledged but scored it as contract fail) | Round 4 + 5 explicitly called out as theater |
| Token spend | ~50-80k per round × 6 | 1.23M single pass |
| Latency | ~10-20 min × 6 = 1h 40min | ~5 min |

relay-review is thorough about rubric compliance. It's not adversarial about invariant surface area. Both styles are useful; neither replaces the other. But right now relay-review's rubric-grep-driven grading reinforces compliance thinking.

## Design options

### Option 1 (minimal): Add an adversarial pass after LGTM
When a round verdicts `lgtm`, run one final `codex exec --sandbox read-only` with the challenge prompt (adversarial, try-to-break, no-compliments, specific file:line). If challenge finds `[P1]` severity issues, demote verdict back to `changes_requested` and feed findings into round N+1's redispatch prompt. Otherwise merge with challenge report attached.

**Pros**: additive, doesn't disrupt rubric-based protocol. Catches exactly what PR #147 landed with.
**Cons**: adds ~5 min + ~1M tokens per PR. Risks "forever round" if challenge always finds something.

### Option 2 (medium): Second-opinion reviewer role
Add a `roles.adversary` field to the relay manifest. Every N-th round (or every round for high-stakes tasks), invoke the adversary alongside the normal reviewer. Verdicts must agree (or adversary's verdict wins if more restrictive).

**Pros**: codifies the two-reviewer pattern. Independent context for adversary prevents rubric-bias.
**Cons**: doubles review token cost. Manifest schema change. Role-binding complexity.

### Option 3 (structural): Challenge-mode rubric factors
Add quality-tier factors keyed on "attack surface" themes: "List 3 paths where this enforcement could be bypassed", "Write a test that attempts to defeat the invariant", etc. Reviewer must answer these explicitly, which forces adversarial framing within the rubric.

**Pros**: no new reviewer role. Rubric authoring becomes the locus of adversarial thinking. Reusable across tasks.
**Cons**: depends on rubric-author discipline. Doesn't catch rubric-grading loopholes (like round 5's grep-pattern compliance).

### Option 4 (hybrid): Challenge-mode as an opt-in tier
Rubric YAML gets a new `challenge:` section listing "try to break" prompts. When set, relay-review runs the normal rubric scoring AND a challenge pass. LGTM requires both to pass.

**Pros**: opt-in per task. High-stakes PRs get adversarial; low-stakes don't pay the cost.
**Cons**: decision load on planner ("do I need challenge mode?"). Easy to forget.

## Recommended next step

1. **Read the gstack-codex skill source** (`~/.claude/skills/gstack-codex/` — specifically the challenge prompt template) and compare against `skills/relay-review/references/reviewer-prompt.md`
2. **Post-mortem PR #147**: take the 9 findings codex produced and ask "what rubric language or review protocol change would have caused relay-review to find each one?" This is the empirical design input.
3. **Prototype Option 1** on a single future PR — measure latency + token cost + marginal finding count vs. baseline
4. **Decide**: adopt Option 1, 2, 3, 4, or "don't adopt" based on prototype data

## Acceptance Criteria

<!-- AC:BEGIN -->
- [ ] Design doc `docs/relay-review-adversarial-benchmark.md` with the 9 findings from PR #147 mapped against "what change would have caught this"
- [ ] Prototype implementation of Option 1 on a feature branch (not merged)
- [ ] Single-PR comparison: run relay-review with and without the adversarial pass, report diff in findings, latency, token cost
- [ ] Decision recorded in `backlog/sprints/_context.md` under "Architecture Decisions" (or new ADR file)
- [ ] If adopted: SKILL.md + reviewer-prompt updated; otherwise: close with rationale
<!-- AC:END -->

## Priority

**Enhancement / idea** — not urgent, but high-leverage. The review process is the trust boundary that gates every PR; improving it compounds.

## Context

- gstack-codex location: `~/.claude/skills/gstack-codex/SKILL.md` (Challenge mode at Step 2B)
- PR #147 adversarial review output captured in session log (2026-04-12, codex 1.23M tokens, 9 findings)
- Related: any Phase 2+ of agentic-patterns-adoption doc

The current challenge review system displays code submissions as plain text, making it difficult for reviewers and learners to quickly identify changes between the original solution and an updated submission. ## NuclearQAv2: A Structured Benchmark for Evaluating Domain-Science Competence in Large Language Models

**Authors:** Henry Shaowu Yuchi, Michal Kucer, Benjamin H. Sims, Selma Peterson, Emily Taylor
**Published:** 2026-06-25
**Categories:** `cs.CL`, `cs.AI`

**Links:** [abs](http://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27047v1) | [pdf](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.27047v1)

---

### Abstract

Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong performance across a wide range of tasks, but ensuring their reliability in highly technical domains remains a significant challenge. In nuclear engineering, problem solving often requires not only factual knowledge but also quantitative reasoning and conceptual understanding. To address the need for systematic evaluation in this domain, we introduce NuclearQAv2, a benchmark for assessing LLMs on nuclear engineering knowledge. The benchmark comprises approximately 1,240 question-answer pairs spanning three categories: boolean, numeric, and verbal. NuclearQAv2 is constructed using a hybrid pipeline that combines expert-authored questions, existing datasets, and LLM-assisted generation from domain-specific technical corpora. By leveraging structured prompting for both automated question generation and response evaluation, the proposed framework enables scalable benchmark construction and evaluation. We evaluate a diverse set of LLMs using NuclearQAv2 and observe substantial performance differences across task types. While the models generally perform well on factual questions, quantitative reasoning and conceptual understanding remain considerably more challenging. These results highlight the importance of multi-faceted evaluation frameworks and establish NuclearQAv2 as a scalable benchmark for assessing LLM capabilities in technical domains.
title: [2606.27047v1] NuclearQAv2: A Structured Benchmark for Evaluating Domain-Science Competence in Large Language Models

---

## Lo scenario

Con la **CSRD** (Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive), decine di migliaia di aziende europee devono divulgare le proprie pratiche di sostenibilità secondo lo standard ESRS — e molte si bloccano già alla prima domanda: *Dove ci collochiamo rispetto al nostro settore?* **ESG-Radar** è un assistente IA che legge le disclosure di sostenibilità, confronta i KPI con i benchmark di settore, assegna un punteggio a lacune e rischi, e produce un report sintetico di CSRD readiness con azioni prioritarie.

| Ruolo | Di cosa si tratta | Inizia qui |
|---|---|---|
| **Sviluppatore/trice IA** | Costruire la pipeline ESG-Radar (Python) + una breve code review | 📂 [`dev/`](./dev/) |

## 🛠️ Percorso Sviluppatore/trice IA

Benvenuto/a. Questo non è un test a trabocchetto. È un piccolo pezzo reale del lavoro che facciamo ogni giorno nel Venture Studio e nell'n8n CoE: costruire qualcosa di utile rapidamente con l'IA.

Non c'è una soluzione modello da raggiungere. Guardiamo come scomponi un problema mal specificato, prendi decisioni e usi l'IA in modo significativo.

### La missione

Costruire un **ESG-Radar**: una piccola pipeline che legge le disclosure di sostenibilità, confronta i KPI con i benchmark di settore, assegna un punteggio a lacune e rischi, e produce un report di readiness sintetico con azioni prioritarie.

Ti forniamo un seed dataset con aziende di esempio (`disclosures.json` / `disclosures.csv`), benchmark di settore (`benchmarks.json`) e alcuni profili individuali. Non è richiesta alcuna conoscenza del dominio — tutti i campi sono documentati ([`../data/README.md`](../data/README.md)) e tutto ciò di cui hai bisogno si trova nel dataset.

> 📂 **Nel repository:** [`../data/`](../data/) con `disclosures.json`, `disclosures.csv`, `benchmarks.json` e profili di esempio (documentazione dei campi: [`../data/README.md`](../data/README.md)). Seed dataset, sintetico/semplificato, aggiornato al 2026-06, non rappresenta una posizione ufficiale di AI:AT.

### Parte A: Costruire il PoC

- **Input:** una o più disclosure (un'azienda per record: settore di attività, settore, emissioni GHG Scope 1/2/3, energia e quota rinnovabile, percentuale di donne nella leadership, numero di dipendenti, tasso di infortuni) più i benchmark di settore corrispondenti.
- **Output:** un report di readiness motivato per azienda: un punteggio (la scala è una tua decisione — giustificala brevemente), un commento «sopra/sotto il benchmark, perché…» per ogni KPI, e 2–3 azioni prioritarie per le lacune più significative.
- **Forma:** un repository Git eseguibile con codice Python reale, e un README che ci permetta di avviarlo in meno di 5 minuti.

> **La decisione di design interessante:** I KPI non sono direttamente comparabili. Le emissioni sono fornite in tonnellate assolute (`ghg_scope1_t_co2e` ecc.), mentre il benchmark è espresso come intensità per dipendente (`benchmark_ghg_intensitaet_t_co2e_pro_ma`). Come normalizzi, con quali KPI inizi, come gestisci i valori mancanti (es. `ghg_scope3 = null`, settore sconosciuto) e come pesi i KPI per ottenere un punteggio: è esattamente lì che vediamo il tuo giudizio. Ci interessa il ragionamento, non una formula prestabilita.

> Una vera chiamata LLM (es. per i testi delle raccomandazioni di azione) è consentita ma non obbligatoria. Un report deterministico o basato su template va benissimo, senza chiave API se non ne hai una. Stack: Python ≥ 3.11 (librerie a scelta libera).

### Parte B: Code review (~15 min)

Ti forniamo un breve snippet Python generato da IA ([`code-review/snippet.py`](./dev/code-review/snippet.py)). Suggerimento: confronta ciò che il commento di documentazione *promette* con ciò che il codice *fa*, e fai attenzione alle unità. C'è un bug funzionale centrale. Trovalo, correggilo e giustifica in 3–5 frasi perché si tratta di un bug. Dicci anche cosa noti nel resto — casi limite mancanti, assunzioni discutibili, validazione assente. Questa critica più ampia conta quanto la correzione stessa. Vogliamo vedere se sai *valutare* il codice IA, non solo generarlo.

> Lo snippet si trova nel file [`./dev/code-review/snippet.py`](./dev/code-review/snippet.py). Non riprodurre il codice nella tua consegna — è sufficiente una spiegazione scritta chiara.

| Funzionalità (funziona, soddisfa il nucleo) | 20% |
| Scomposizione e giudizio (ambiguità risolta sensatamente, buoni trade-off) | 20% |

---

## 📊 Percorso Analista IA & Venture Builder

Benvenuto/a. Questo è un pezzo reale di lavoro in un Venture Studio: valutare la maturità commerciale di un'idea e renderla vendibile — in una settimana, con l'IA come leva.

Il nostro team tecnico sta costruendo un prototipo: ESG-Radar, un assistente IA che legge le disclosure di sostenibilità di un'azienda, le confronta con i benchmark di settore, assegna un punteggio a lacune e rischi di compliance, e produce in pochi minuti un report di CSRD readiness con azioni prioritarie. La pressione di mercato è chiara: la **CSRD** obbliga decine di migliaia di aziende europee a divulgare la propria sostenibilità secondo lo standard ESRS, e molte non sanno dove si trovano. Il tuo compito: è un business? E come lo portiamo sul mercato?

Ti forniamo come orientamento un seed dataset (aziende di esempio con KPI ESG in JSON/CSV più benchmark di settore; il CSV si apre comodamente in Excel/Sheets). *Ti mostra il tipo di dati con cui ESG-Radar lavora. I tuoi clienti paganti sono le aziende che devono diventare CSRD-ready.*

> ⚠️ **Importante per il sizing:** I dati non contengono deliberatamente cifre di mercato, prezzi o conversione (mostrano solo KPI di esempio). Il numero di clienti raggiungibili, il prezzo e la conversione li ricerchi o stimi tu stesso/a — l'IA e il web sono esattamente lì per questo (fonti gradite). Le aziende di esempio servono ad affinare il tuo ICP/segmento, non a derivare volumi.

Per questa analisi, tratta ESG-Radar come un venture commerciale autonomo, separato dal contesto AI:AT (non commerciale, finanziato dall'UE).

## Fable task

Run one artifact-only strategic research pass for Pixel Nations.

This is not a UI audit. This is not a vertical-slice polish pass. The goal is to challenge whether Pixel Nations is on the best possible path toward becoming an outstanding strategy game.

## Real goal

We want to create a genuinely excellent strategy game — ideally one of the best browser-first strategy games in the world over time.

Pixel Nations is our current concept and direction, but it is not sacred. If the current direction is weak, too narrow, too cosmetic, or not strategic enough, say so.

## Current Pixel Nations direction

- Browser-first strategy game.
- World has 10,000 finite lands.
- Current demo sector: Sector A-01 / Aurelian Basin.
- Current high-level arc: land -> settlement/city -> nation -> empire.
- Current product truth: one land can become an empire.
- Avoid crypto, NFT, wallet, token, mint, pay-to-win, backend-first, real multiplayer-first, payment-first, or infrastructure-first direction.
- Tiny-team MVP constraint: simple first, deep later.

## Important correction

Do not over-focus on phrases like “founding moment” or “the player was first and history remembers it.” Those can be useful emotional hooks, but they are not the goal.

The goal is great strategy gameplay.

We need real strategic decisions, meaningful tradeoffs, map pressure, long-term ambition, replayability, readable systems, and a path from simple MVP to deep game.

## Benchmark games to analyze

Break down the best useful ingredients from, at minimum:

- Civilization series: exploration, expansion, one-more-turn pacing, technology/culture progress, readable empire growth.
- Crusader Kings: characters, dynasty, relations, emergent stories, soft power.
- Europa Universalis / grand strategy: map pressure, geopolitics, tradeoffs across decades, diplomacy, national identity.
- Tribal Wars / Plemiona: simple browser map, territorial competition, asynchronous pressure, easy entry, social coordination.
- Anno / Settlers: settlement growth, production chains, visual prosperity, spatial economy.
- Factorio / Mindustry: system clarity, automation, routing, resource pressure, defense/optimization loops.
- Total War: empire layer plus conflict fantasy, readable military pressure.
- Clash of Clans / Boom Beach: accessible base actions, short sessions, timers, clear upgrades, mobile command clarity.

Do not copy these games. Extract ingredients and evaluate what Pixel Nations should learn from them.

## Required output

1. Brutal verdict: is current Pixel Nations direction strong enough to become an excellent strategy game, or does it need a major pivot?
2. What is strategically strong about the current idea?
3. What is weak, fake, cosmetic, or at risk of becoming a shallow map UI?
4. Best strategy-game ingredients Pixel Nations should borrow, grouped by source game.
5. Which ingredients are dangerous or too expensive for MVP.
6. 3 to 5 alternative possible game directions, for example:
   - atlas empire builder,
   - browser grand strategy,
   - territory-control strategy,
   - settlement-to-nation economic sim,
   - asynchronous world strategy,
   - hybrid city builder plus geopolitical map.
7. Score each direction from 1 to 10 on:
   - strategic depth potential,
   - MVP feasibility,
   - uniqueness,
   - browser fit,
   - future business potential,
   - first-session fun,
   - long-term replayability.
8. Recommend one direction and explain why.
9. Define the core strategic loop for that direction.
10. Define what the first 10 minutes should feel like if the game is actually fun, not just pretty.
11. Define the first 2 implementation sprints we should do next.
12. Define what we should stop building immediately.
13. Define what Cursor should not touch until the strategic direction is settled.
14. Give one concise decision line:
    `DECISION: STAY_THE_COURSE / PIVOT_WITHIN_PIXEL_NATIONS / MAJOR_RETHINK_REQUIRED`

## Hard constraints

- No blockchain, NFT, wallet, token, mint, pay-to-win.
- No backend-first plan.
- No real multiplayer-first dependency.
- No “build everything” plan.
- No generic inspirational slogans.
- No vague founding-moment-only answer.
- No expensive art/game engine pivot unless the argument is overwhelming.
- Optimize for a tiny team that can create a compelling browser MVP, then deepen it.

## Desired tone

Be direct, skeptical, and ambitious. Act like a senior strategy-game director who wants Pixel Nations to become truly excellent, not merely coherent.

Overview
Your goal is to create a [terminal bench](https://www.tbench.ai/) task using the [Harbor framework](https://harborframework.com/docs/tasks/task-tutorial). The terminal bench is a crowdsourced benchmark that measures an agent's ability to perform tasks using the terminal, and the Harbor framework makes it easy to create these tasks. We hope that this is a fun exercise that also serves as a good starting point for understanding RL environments! 

What makes a good task?
Generally, a good task is one that is challenging to the model (measured by the pass rate for a frontier model - Claude Opus 4.6) but not unsolvable, realistic (simulates a meaningful, real-world use case), unhackable (the model has to perform the task correctly to get a reward, and there should be no pathway for the model to game the reward), and reproducible (for a given sequence of model actions on the environment, the reward should be the same). We would like to see a novel task relevant to software engineering. This task must not exist in previous benchmark versions or be contained in an open contribution to this benchmark; in other words, we seek an original scenario that you conceived. Beyond this, we encourage you to read up on and understand the benchmark further, and to use your judgment to determine a good task. 

Deliverable
Fork this repository: https://github.com/harbor-framework/terminal-bench-3/, and create a PR with your task in your own fork. The README and CIs in this repository, as well as other contributions, should give you a good sense of how to contribute. We don't expect you to make a contribution to the actual terminal bench 3 effort, although you are welcome to do so! Just a PR against your own fork works for this assessment. 

During our interview
We will review your PR and discuss your task: what makes it a good task in your view, how you verified its high quality, and how you would expand upon it. Please share this PR at least one hour before the interview so we have time to review it beforehand.
